notes.bp: A recording may contain an unknown number of people speaking at once, but a useful separator must decide how many voices to return.
notes.wh: A fixed two- or three-speaker model fails when more people are present, while a separate model for each count grows expensive.
notes.naive: Tell the model the speaker count in advance, or select a decoder built for that count.
notes.ap: Separate one stream at a time and let a lightweight authorization block decide when recursion should stop.
notes.mech: ReSepNet applies a dual-path transformer repeatedly; each iteration estimates one source and cross-correlation decides whether another iteration is needed. It trains on two/three-speaker mixtures and tests on four/five.
notes.math: Permutation-invariant loss ignores output order. SI-SNR improvement is 21.16 dB on WSJ0-2mix, 19.19 on 3mix, 14.91 on 4mix, and 12.03 on 5mix; the 2.8M-parameter model estimates count with 96.6% accuracy.
notes.dots: The stopping rule becomes part of separation rather than an external assumption, connecting source separation to a real deployment interface.
notes.ww: The paper reports higher SI-SNR improvement than listed baselines and generalization from two/three-speaker training to four/five-speaker tests.
notes.limits: The evidence is synthetic WSJ0 mixtures, 8-kHz four-second windows, and a bounded count range; real rooms and end-to-end recognition are not tested. Results are author-reported.

notes.bp: A physical vocal-tract model should either hold a known shape still for teaching or change shape over time to demonstrate articulation.
notes.wh: A static model is repeatable but cannot show movement; a dynamic machine is expressive but harder to build and interpret.
notes.naive: Use one simplified tube model for every purpose and ignore the missing detail or motion.
notes.ap: Show the two ends of the design space: a fixed one-vowel dummy head and a cam-driven model whose blocks change shape in real time.
notes.mech: The static model fixes one tract configuration and radiates a repeatable vowel; the dynamic model uses blocks and cams to change simulated articulators and tract shape.
notes.math: The relevant object is tract geometry, which determines resonances and radiation; this demonstration has no common benchmark score.
notes.dots: It makes the production-side source/filter relationship visible instead of hiding it in a learned representation.
notes.ww: The paper demonstrates both models and argues that static and dynamic versions serve different education, phonetics, pathology, and technology purposes.
notes.limits: This is a two-page demonstration with no shared quantitative evaluation or claim of human-speech equivalence.

notes.bp: A language-identification system should identify the language, not the speaker's accent or first language.
notes.wh: Short phonetic patterns associated with a speaker's native language can make a model confuse accent with language; overall accuracy hides minority failure.
notes.naive: Train a classifier on whole-utterance labels and assume longer audio automatically supplies enough language evidence.
notes.ap: Add phoneme-sequence or discretized-unit views and test the shortcut by permuting short speech chunks.
notes.mech: The study compares ECAPA-TDNN, MMS, and GEO systems on several corpora, measures accent-language confusion, reverses chunks, and fuses acoustic and sequence representations.
notes.math: ECAPA-TDNN falls from 87.6% to 55.8% on CommonVoice and 73% to 57% on EdAcc for mainstream versus L2 accents; many models remain stable down to roughly 0.25-second chunks.
notes.dots: Accent robustness is a representation problem: retain language-level sequence structure while discarding the shortcut correlating accent with language.
notes.ww: Dutch-accented English is called Dutch in 82.6% of errors in one setting; sequence-aware systems reduce this confusion while retaining mainstream performance.
notes.limits: Datasets, accent categories, chunking, and aggregation define the result; it diagnoses a shortcut but does not prove cultural neutrality or universal transfer.

notes.bp: A recognizer trained on typical speech must understand speech altered by different medical conditions despite scarce labels.
notes.wh: Articulation, phonation, and prosody change differently by etiology; indiscriminate data may teach the wrong invariances, while synthetic data adds artifacts.
notes.naive: Fine-tune a general encoder on the small clinical corpus, or add as much unrelated speech as possible.
notes.ap: Continue self-supervised pre-training on pathological speech, use etiology-specific codebooks, and select external examples by semantic similarity.
notes.mech: A BEST-RQ Conformer is continued on pathological speech; fine-tuning compares synthetic, out-of-domain, and transcript-embedding-selected data, with similarity losses.
notes.math: Overall WER is 19.73 versus 22.73 for the BEST-RQ baseline; 150% OOD augmentation reaches 17.32 and similarity-weighted pairing 17.81, while Down syndrome does not benefit from augmentation.
notes.dots: Variation is structured rather than noise: useful extra data resemble the production differences the recognizer must serve.
notes.ww: The authors report 13.2% relative WER improvement from pathology-aware pre-training, up to 8.7% from synthetic data, 12.2% from OOD data, and 9.7% from semantic selection.
notes.limits: Etiologies, corpora, similarity model, and ratios bound the claim; improvements differ by condition and synthetic speech may not preserve clinical variation.

notes.bp: TTS must sound natural and intelligible while responding quickly enough for real use; diffusion refinement makes that balance difficult.
notes.wh: Maximizing a learned naturalness reward can move the generator away from the distribution learned during diffusion training.
notes.naive: Maximize perceptual reward alone, or keep the original loss and accept the quality-speed tradeoff.
notes.ap: Use the diffusion loss as a regularizer inside policy optimization so naturalness improvement remains tied to learned speech structure.
notes.mech: DLPO fine-tunes WaveGrad 2 with a reward combining UTMOS naturalness and the original diffusion loss, comparing DPOK, KLinR, and diffusion-only optimization.
notes.math: DLPO reports UTMOS 3.65, NISQA 4.02, WER 1.0%, and 67% pairwise preference; these are different proxies, not one quality axis.
notes.dots: The control problem is preserving content while changing delivery; here stability comes from constraining the generator's own probability structure.
notes.ww: The paper reports gains over the baseline and competing reward objectives, with listeners preferring samples 67% of the time.
notes.limits: The evidence uses WaveGrad 2 and selected reward predictors; predicted metrics and pairwise preference do not establish broad real-time deployment.

notes.bp: An audio-language system should answer different questions about the same sound, not memorize one caption wording.
notes.wh: Several captions can describe one sound, and direct reference-sentence training can reward surface wording rather than scene meaning.
notes.naive: Train directly to reproduce the dataset caption and assume fluency implies instruction following.
notes.ap: Train the model to continue a dialogue after an audio-triggered caption, making the target a conversational response.
notes.mech: An audio encoder feeds an adapter and language model; interleaved audio/text examples use token cross-entropy, with LoRA tested on AudioCaps, WavCaps, and Clotho.
notes.math: The loss is token-level cross-entropy. The best reported average AQA accuracy is 47.70%, judged by Llama-3-70B-Instruct; the judge is itself a proxy.
notes.dots: The move is from naming an event to grounding an answer in it, connecting caption variation to useful interaction.
notes.ww: Dialogue-continuation training enables zero-shot instruction following and improves reported AQA, while AAC gains are mixed.
notes.limits: Generated captions, benchmarks, and an LLM judge define the evidence; human usefulness for deaf or hard-of-hearing users is not established.

notes.bp: A fake-speech detector must recognize manipulation it has not seen, including changed codec, attack, and language.
notes.wh: A detector can learn a generator or recording fingerprint instead of the genuine/fake property, so in-domain scores collapse under shift.
notes.naive: Train on known attacks and treat high test accuracy as general spoofing ability.
notes.ap: Remove attack-specific information with an attack-invariant encoder-decoder and common-subspace decomposition before classification.
notes.mech: A frozen wav2vec2 front-end and AASIST backend produce embeddings; AIED suppresses attack variation and CSD projects into a shared subspace, tested on ASVspoof and IndicTTS.
notes.math: EER changes from 6.14 to 5.84 on LA, 12.33 to 10.90 on DF, and 59.82 to 39.51 on IndicTTS; the large cross-language gap remains.
notes.dots: Security claims require invariance to attack and language shortcuts while retaining the genuine/fake distinction.
notes.ww: The paper reports 4%, 12%, and 34% relative EER improvements on LA, DF, and IndicTTS, with ablations separating AIED and CSD.
notes.limits: Datasets, attacks, frozen front-end, and language coverage bound the result; IndicTTS EER remains high and no independent adversarial evaluation was performed.

notes.bp: A child-focused ASR service may receive speech over time, but updating it can make it forget earlier speakers and require centralized storage.
notes.wh: Children's speech changes with development, data are scarce, and sequential speakers create drift; ordinary fine-tuning overwrites useful parameters.
notes.naive: Fine-tune the latest model on each new batch and keep only the newest checkpoint.
notes.ap: Protect parameters important for earlier batches with EWC or SI, and compare online checkpoint-selection policies.
notes.mech: Whisper-small trains on ten sequential MyST batches. EWC adds an importance-weighted quadratic penalty; SI accumulates importance from parameter movement and loss reduction; models use no selection, rolling-window, or best-so-far selection.
notes.math: MyST has 145.54 training hours, 23.09 development hours, and 25.05 test hours. EWC and SI report relative WER reductions of 5.21% and 4.36% against sequential fine-tuning; bootstrap intervals quantify uncertainty.
notes.dots: Adaptation becomes a memory-allocation problem: retain old acoustic-to-word mappings while making room for new children and privacy-conscious data arrival.
notes.ww: EWC and SI keep WER more stable across ten batches and improve over ordinary sequential fine-tuning under the protocol.
notes.limits: The protocol is simulated from MyST, uses English child speech and Whisper-small, and treats parameter importance as a proxy rather than a privacy guarantee.
